title: AI is entering financial guidance as a low-cost research layer without becoming a trusted decision-maker
source_unit: Gallup and Edward Jones Financial Fulfillment study, public article on where Americans seek financial guidance
geography: United States; adults age 21 and older; survey fielded March 20-April 6, 2026

observations.period: March 20-April 6, 2026; sources used by U.S. financial-guidance seekers

guidance_reach.unit: percent who sought financial guidance from at least one source in the prior year

internet_research.unit: percent of guidance-seekers using their own internet research

ai_use.unit: percent of guidance-seekers using AI tools such as ChatGPT or Claude

access_route.value: AI and open internet research can lower the cost and friction of entering a financial-learning journey, but use should not be read as trust or completed financial action.

observations.method: Gallup and Edward Jones survey of 5,075 U.S. adults age 21 and older, conducted March 20-April 6, 2026, using Gallup's probability-based panel; public article reports source-use percentages.
observations.uncertainty: The public article does not provide the full questionnaire, weighting details, question order, or observed financial decisions; percentages describe reported guidance-seeking, not realized financial welfare.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults seeking financial guidance; source-use patterns vary by generation and financial fulfillment category.
observations.counterinterpretation: Internet and AI use may supplement professional or family advice rather than substitute for it; self-directed research can reflect curiosity, affordability constraints, or a need to verify advice.

observations.period: March 20-April 6, 2026; reported trust versus use of financial-guidance sources

professional_use.unit: percent of guidance-seekers using professional financial advisers

family_use.unit: percent using a parent, sibling or relative

advisor_confidence.value: about eight in ten U.S. adults have at least some confidence in financial advisers

trust_use_gap.value: The most-used source is not the most trusted source: internet research is widely used, while professional advice has higher confidence but lower reported use.

observations.method: Descriptive survey estimates reported by Gallup from the same probability-based U.S. adult sample.
observations.uncertainty: The public release does not establish why people choose a source, whether professional advice is financially accessible, or whether trust predicts better outcomes.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults across financially fulfilled, conflicted and stressed categories; the public article reports different source mixes by financial situation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Professional advice may be used less because it is unnecessary for simple questions or costly to access, not because people reject human expertise.

observations.period: March 20-April 6, 2026; age gradient in AI financial-guidance use and confidence

denominator.unit: U.S. adults surveyed by Gallup; subgroup estimates reported by generation

younger_ai_use.value: about one in four Gen Z adults and millennials who sought guidance used AI, compared with 7% of baby boomers

ai_confidence.value: 36% of millennials and 32% of Gen Z adults reported at least some confidence in AI tools, versus 27% of Gen Xers and 15% of baby boomers
ai_confidence.unit: percent reporting some or greater confidence

human_fallback.value: Even among younger adults who use AI more, confidence remains below a majority, leaving human networks and professional accountability as open decision-stage complements.

observations.method: Gallup subgroup comparisons reported from the 2026 U.S. survey; generation definitions and full cross-tabs are not reproduced in the public article.
observations.uncertainty: The age gradient is descriptive; it does not show cohort, life-stage, income, education, or task-complexity causation, nor whether AI use improves financial outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Gen Z adults, millennials, Gen Xers and baby boomers who seek financial guidance.
observations.counterinterpretation: Younger adults may use AI because they face lower-cost access constraints or different financial questions, while older adults may have more established adviser relationships.

related_sources.claim: Official Gallup article reports the sample, field dates, source-use estimates, confidence gap and generational comparisons.

boundary: This record adds a financial-guidance trust-and-access route: AI and internet research are low-friction entry points, while professional and human-network sources retain greater confidence for consequential decisions. It does not establish advice quality, financial outcomes, fiduciary protection, or causal substitution between AI and human guidance.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Gallup article was reviewed for sample, field dates, source-use percentages, confidence comparisons, financial-fulfillment framing and generational estimates.
